decisions.choice: answered and said: the usual opening of a speech
decisions.reason: "He answered and said" opens each speech in the dialogue (3:2; 6:1). Job answers Bildad's short speech of chapter 25.

decisions.choice: how far Job's speech runs: through chapter 31, though 27:1 and 29:1 open new parts
decisions.reason: In the book as it stands Job speaks from here to the end of chapter 31; 27:1 and 29:1 add a new heading ("Job again took up his discourse"). Because Bildad's speech is so short and Zophar has no third speech, some think parts of chapters 26 and 27 once belonged to the friends (see 26:5). The text gives these words to Job.

decisions.choice: answered (B) / said (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use one English verb for the Hebrew pair, as in the other speech introductions of Job. The introduction stays prose.

records.literal_gloss: How you have helped [one with] no power! [How] you have saved [the] arm [with] no strength!

en.L: How you have helped [one with] no power! \q [How] you have saved [the] arm [with] no strength!
en.B: How you have helped the powerless! \q How you have saved the arm that has no strength!
en.R: What a help you have been to someone who is weak! \q What a rescue for someone who has no strength!

decisions.choice: biting irony: Bildad has helped no one
decisions.reason: Job's exclamations are sarcastic. Bildad claimed to speak for God, but his words gave no help to the weak man in front of him. The "you" is singular: Job answers Bildad (chapter 25).

decisions.choice: the arm: strength to act
decisions.reason: In Hebrew the arm stands for a person's power (22:8-9; Psalm 10:15). "An arm with no strength" is someone helpless, here Job himself.

decisions.choice: someone who is weak ... someone who has no strength
decisions.reason: Readable turns the picture of the arm into the person it stands for (m2) and keeps the ironic exclamations.

source.text: מַה־יָּ֭עַצְתָּ לְלֹ֣א חָכְמָ֑ה וְ֝תוּשִׁיָּ֗ה לָרֹ֥ב הוֹדָֽעְתָּ׃

records.literal_gloss: How you have counseled [one with] no wisdom! And sound wisdom in abundance you have made known!

en.L: How you have counseled [one with] no wisdom, \q and made known sound wisdom in abundance!
en.B: How you have advised one who lacks wisdom, \q and shown such a wealth of insight!
en.R: What good advice you have given to someone with no wisdom! \q How much insight you have shared!

decisions.choice: more irony: Bildad's counsel was empty
decisions.reason: Job goes on in the same sarcastic tone as verse 2. The "abundance" Bildad made known was five verses that only repeated what had been said before (25:4-6; compare 4:17; 15:14-16).

decisions.choice: sound wisdom: practical insight that leads to success
decisions.reason: The word (tushiyyah) means effective wisdom, the kind that works (5:12; 6:13; 11:6). Job says Bildad offered a great deal of it, and means he offered none.

decisions.choice: such a wealth of insight
decisions.reason: Balanced says "insight" for the second word for wisdom so the line does not repeat "wisdom", and "such a wealth" keeps the mock praise.

source.text: אֶת־מִ֭י הִגַּ֣דְתָּ מִלִּ֑ין וְנִשְׁמַת־מִ֝י יָצְאָ֥ה מִמֶּֽךָּ׃

records.literal_gloss: With whom have you told words? And the breath of whom has gone out from you?

en.L: With whom have you uttered words? \q And whose breath has gone out from you?
en.B: With whose help have you uttered these words? \q Whose spirit has spoken through you?
en.R: Who helped you say these things? \q Whose spirit was speaking through you?

decisions.choice: with whom: with whose help
decisions.reason: The word ('et) can mean "with" (by whose help) or mark the one spoken to (to whom). Set beside the second line, which asks whose breath came out of Bildad, it most likely asks who stood behind his words.

decisions.choice: breath: the breath or spirit that inspires speech
decisions.reason: The word (neshamah) is the breath of life (27:3; 32:8; 33:4), and can be the breath or spirit that moves a person to speak. Job asks mockingly whether some spirit spoke through Bildad, as Eliphaz claimed a spirit spoke to him (4:15-16). He implies that Bildad's words came from no one but himself.

decisions.choice: Whose spirit has spoken through you?
alternatives: Whose breath has gone out from you?
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "spirit" and "spoken through" to make clear that the breath is what inspires the speech (m2). Literal keeps the picture of breath going out.

decisions.choice: Whose spirit was speaking through you?
alternatives: Whose breath has gone out from you?
decisions.reason: As Balanced (m2).

records.literal_gloss: The shades are made to tremble beneath [the] waters and those dwelling in them.

en.L: The shades writhe \q beneath [the] waters and those who dwell in them.
en.B: The spirits of the dead tremble, \q those beneath the waters and all who live there.
en.R: The dead shake with fear \q in the deep places under the waters, with all who live there.

decisions.choice: the shades: the dead in the world below
decisions.reason: The word (repha'im) names the shadowy dead in Sheol (Psalm 88:11; Proverbs 9:18; Isaiah 14:9). The same word is used elsewhere for a people of giants (Deuteronomy 2:11), but here, next to Sheol and Abaddon (verse 6), it means the dead.

decisions.choice: beneath the waters: the world of the dead under the deep
decisions.reason: In the Bible's picture of the world, the waters of the deep lie under the earth, and the realm of the dead lies deeper still (38:16-17). Even there God's power is felt and the dead tremble before him.

decisions.choice: Job takes up the theme of God's power in creation, 26:5-14
alternatives: these verses continue Bildad's speech of chapter 25
decisions.reason: Verses 5-14 praise God's power over the deep, the sky and the sea, much as Bildad praised it in 25:2-3. Because Bildad's speech is so short, some think these verses once belonged to it. In the text as it stands Job speaks them, and they fit his own praise of God's power in 9:5-10 and 12:13-25: he can describe God's greatness as well as his friends can.

decisions.choice: the spirits of the dead (B) / the dead (R)
decisions.reason: "Shades" is a rare word in modern English. Balanced and Readable say what it means (m1); Literal keeps "shades".

source.text: עָר֣וֹם שְׁא֣וֹל נֶגְדּ֑וֹ וְאֵ֥ין כְּ֝ס֗וּת לָֽאֲבַדּֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: Naked [is] Sheol before him, and there is not a covering for Abaddon.

en.L: Sheol [is] naked before {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, \q and there is no covering for Abaddon.
en.B: Sheol lies naked before {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}; \q Abaddon has no covering.
en.R: The grave is wide open to God. \q The place of destruction has nothing to hide it.

decisions.choice: Sheol: the place of the dead
decisions.reason: Sheol is the world of the dead, pictured as deep under the earth (7:9; 11:8; 17:13). It is the deepest and darkest place there is, and still it lies open to God's sight (Psalm 139:8; Proverbs 15:11).

decisions.choice: Abaddon: the place of destruction, another name for the realm of the dead
decisions.reason: Abaddon ('avaddon) comes from the verb "to perish" and means "destruction". In Job it stands beside Sheol and death as a name for the place of the dead (28:22; 31:12; compare Proverbs 15:11; Psalm 88:12). Revelation 9:11 later uses the name for the angel of the abyss. The name stays "Abaddon" at Literal and Balanced.

decisions.choice: naked, no covering: fully seen by God
decisions.reason: Nothing hides the world of the dead from God; he sees it as plainly as an uncovered body (compare 24:7, where the same words describe the poor with no covering against the cold).

decisions.choice: the grave / the place of destruction
decisions.reason: Readable says "the grave" for Sheol and "the place of destruction" for Abaddon, as elsewhere in Job (m1, m2).

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Readable names God so the reader knows who sees.

source.text: נֹטֶ֣ה צָפ֣וֹן עַל־תֹּ֑הוּ תֹּ֥לֶה אֶ֝֗רֶץ עַל־בְּלִי־מָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: [He is] stretching out [the] north over emptiness, [he is] hanging [the] earth on nothing.

en.L: He stretches out [the] north over emptiness; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} hangs [the] earth on nothing.
en.B: He stretches out the northern sky over empty space; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} hangs the earth on nothing.
en.R: God spreads out the northern sky over empty space. \q He hangs the earth on nothing at all.

decisions.choice: the north: the northern sky, or the high mountain of the north
decisions.reason: The word (tsafon) means the north. Here it is something God "stretches out" over the void, the verb used of spreading out the heavens like a tent (9:8; Isaiah 40:22). So it is most likely the northern sky. The north was also where the old poems placed the high mountain of the gods (Isaiah 14:13; Psalm 48:3), and that picture may lie behind the word.

decisions.choice: emptiness: the formless void
decisions.reason: The word (tohu) is the "formless" of Genesis 1:2: empty, shapeless space. God has set the heavens over it.

decisions.choice: hangs the earth on nothing: the earth needs no support but God
decisions.reason: "On not-anything" (beli mah) means on nothing at all. The point is God's power: the earth rests on nothing but his will. Elsewhere the Bible pictures the earth on foundations or pillars (9:6; 38:4-6); the poems use more than one picture, and this one stresses that nothing holds the world up except God.

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Readable names God at the start of the hymn so the reader knows who is described.

records.literal_gloss: [He is] binding up waters in his clouds, and not is split open [the] cloud under them.

en.L: He binds up waters in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clouds, \q and [the] cloud does not split open under them.
en.B: He wraps up the waters in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clouds, \q yet the clouds do not burst under their weight.
en.R: He wraps up the rain in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clouds, \q and they do not burst open under all that water.

decisions.choice: binds up waters in his clouds: holds the rain in the clouds like water in a skin
decisions.reason: The verb (tsarar) means to tie up in a bundle or bag (Proverbs 30:4: "who has bound up the waters in a garment?"). The clouds are pictured as water-skins that God fills (38:37). That such thin things hold so much water without tearing shows his power.

decisions.choice: under their weight
decisions.reason: "Under them" means under the waters they hold. Balanced says "under their weight" and Readable "under all that water" so the picture is clear.

records.literal_gloss: [He is] covering [the] face of [the] throne; he spreads over it his cloud.

en.L: He covers [the] face of [the] throne; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} spreads {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} cloud over it.
en.B: He veils the face of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} throne, \q spreading {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} cloud over it.
en.R: He hides {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} throne from view \q by spreading {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clouds over it.

decisions.choice: the throne: God's throne in the heavens, hidden by cloud
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text points the word as "throne" (kisseh, here in an unusual spelling). God's throne is above the sky, and the clouds hide it from human eyes (22:13-14; Psalm 97:2). Spelled with the same letters but pointed differently, the word is "full moon" (Psalm 81:4; Proverbs 7:20), which also fits: God covers the face of the moon with cloud. This translation follows the pointing of the Hebrew text.

decisions.choice: spreads: spreads out
decisions.reason: The verb form (parshez) is found only here; it is most likely a form of the common verb "to spread out" (parash).

decisions.choice: his throne
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "his throne", since it is God's throne in the heavens (m1); Literal keeps "the throne" as the Hebrew has it.

records.literal_gloss: A limit he has drawn as a circle on [the] face of [the] waters, to [the] end of light with darkness.

en.L: He has drawn a limit as a circle on [the] face of [the] waters, \q at [the] boundary of light with darkness.
en.B: He has marked out a circle on the face of the waters \q as a boundary between light and darkness.
en.R: He drew a circle on the surface of the sea \q to mark where light ends and darkness begins.

decisions.choice: a circle on the face of the waters: the horizon
decisions.reason: The picture is of God drawing a line round the edge of the world sea (Proverbs 8:27: "when he drew a circle on the face of the deep"). Where the sky meets the sea, at the horizon, is the edge of the world of light; beyond it lies darkness.

decisions.choice: a limit: a fixed boundary God has set
decisions.reason: The word (choq) means something laid down: a decree, a portion, or a boundary (14:5; 38:10). Here it is the limit God marked out, past which the light does not go.

decisions.choice: to the end of light with darkness: as far as the point where light meets darkness
decisions.reason: "The end of light with darkness" is the place where daylight stops and darkness starts, the edge of the circle.

decisions.choice: marked out a circle ... as a boundary
alternatives: drawn a limit as a circle
decisions.reason: Balanced puts "circle" first and turns "limit" into "boundary" in the second line, which is easier to follow in English.

records.literal_gloss: [The] pillars of heaven shake, and they are astounded at his rebuke.

en.L: [The] pillars of heaven shake, \q and they are astounded at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} rebuke.
en.B: The pillars of heaven tremble \q and are stunned at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} rebuke.
en.R: The pillars that hold up the sky shake. \q They are terrified when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} shouts at them.

decisions.choice: the pillars of heaven: the great mountains thought to hold up the sky
decisions.reason: The poem pictures the sky as a vault resting on pillars at the edge of the earth, perhaps the high mountains on the horizon (compare 9:6, the pillars of the earth; 2 Samuel 22:8). When God speaks in anger, even what holds up the heavens shakes.

decisions.choice: rebuke: an angry shout, like thunder
decisions.reason: God's "rebuke" (ge'arah) is often a roar that drives back the sea and shakes the world (Psalm 18:16; 104:7; Isaiah 50:2). In storm it is heard as thunder (verse 14).

decisions.choice: when he shouts at them
decisions.reason: Readable says what a rebuke is here (m2).

source.text: בְּ֭כֹחוֹ רָגַ֣ע הַיָּ֑ם וּ֝בִתְבוּנָת֗וֹ מָ֣חַץ רָֽהַב׃

records.literal_gloss: By his power he stirred up the sea, and by his understanding he smashed Rahab.

en.L: By {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} power {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} stirred up the sea, \q and by {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} understanding {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} smashed Rahab.
en.B: By {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} power {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} stirred up the sea; \q by {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} skill {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} struck Rahab down.
en.R: By {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} power {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} stirred up the sea. \q By {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} wisdom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} crushed Rahab, the monster of the sea.

decisions.choice: stirred up: roused the sea
decisions.reason: The verb (raga') can mean to stir up (Isaiah 51:15; Jeremiah 31:35, both of God stirring up the sea so that its waves roar) or, in another use, to be at rest. Read the first way, God shows his power by rousing the sea; read the second, by bringing it to stillness. Both show that the sea is under his control, and the second line goes on to his victory over the sea monster.

decisions.choice: Rahab: the sea monster of chaos (9:13)
decisions.reason: On Rahab see 9:13. In the old poems God defeated the monster of the sea at the beginning (Psalm 89:11; Isaiah 51:9). Here Job sets Rahab beside the sea itself: God masters the raging deep.

decisions.choice: understanding: God's skill and insight
decisions.reason: God's "understanding" (tevunah) is the skilled wisdom by which he made and orders the world (Proverbs 3:19; Jeremiah 10:12). It is set beside his power.

decisions.choice: the monster of the sea
decisions.reason: Readable adds who Rahab is (m2), so the reader does not think of Rahab of Jericho.

source.text: בְּ֭רוּחוֹ שָׁמַ֣יִם שִׁפְרָ֑ה חֹֽלֲלָ֥ה יָ֝ד֗וֹ נָחָ֥שׁ בָּרִֽיחַ׃

records.literal_gloss: By his wind [the] heavens [are] clearness; it pierced, his hand, [the] serpent fleeing.

en.L: By {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} wind [the] heavens [are] fair; \q {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hand pierced the fleeing serpent.
en.B: By {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} breath the skies became clear; \q {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hand pierced the fleeing serpent.
en.R: He breathed, and the sky was clear again. \q With {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own hand {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} stabbed the serpent as it tried to escape.

decisions.choice: wind: God's wind or breath
decisions.reason: The word (ruach) means wind, breath or spirit. In this storm scene it is most likely the wind God sends, which sweeps the clouds away and leaves the sky clear (37:21). "His breath" says the same thing in the language of a person: God breathes and the storm clears.

decisions.choice: clearness: fair, bright sky
decisions.reason: The word (shifrah) is found only here and comes from a root meaning to be fair or bright. The heavens become clear after the storm.

decisions.choice: the fleeing serpent: the sea monster, also called Leviathan
decisions.reason: Isaiah 27:1 calls Leviathan "the fleeing serpent" and says God will punish it with his sword. The fleeing serpent here is the same chaos monster as Rahab in verse 12 and Leviathan in 3:8. Some think of a serpent seen in the stars, swept from sight by the storm, but the parallel with Isaiah makes the sea monster more likely.

decisions.choice: breath (B) / breathed (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "breath", which keeps the link between God's wind and his breath (m1); Literal says "wind".

decisions.choice: as it tried to escape
decisions.reason: Readable says what "fleeing" means here: the monster was trying to get away.

source.text: הֶן־אֵ֤לֶּה׀קְצ֬וֹת דְּרָכָ֗יו וּמַה־שֵּׁ֣מֶץ דָּ֭בָר נִשְׁמַע־בּ֑וֹ וְרַ֥עַם גְּ֝בוּרוֹתָ֗יומִ֣י יִתְבּוֹנָֽן׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Look, these [are the] edges of his ways, and what a whisper of a word we hear of him! And the thunder of his mighty deeds, who will understand?

en.L: Look, these [are the] edges of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} ways, \q and what a whisper of a word we hear of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}! \q But the thunder of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mighty deeds, who can understand?
en.B: Look, these are only the outer edges of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} ways; \q how faint the whisper we hear of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}! \q But the thunder of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} power, who can understand it?
en.R: And these are only the edges of what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} does. \q We hear only a whisper about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. \q Who could ever understand {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mighty power, which is like thunder?

decisions.choice: the edges of his ways: only the outskirts of what God does
decisions.reason: The word (qetsot) means the ends or fringes of something. All that Job has described, the deep, the sky, the sea, is only the outer edge of God's works (compare Proverbs 8:22, where wisdom is the beginning of his way).

decisions.choice: a whisper of a word: a faint sound, as against thunder
decisions.reason: The word (shemets) means a whisper or faint trace (4:12). What humans hear of God is only a whisper; the full "thunder" of his might is beyond them.

decisions.choice: the thunder of his mighty deeds: the full force of God's power
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) and the reading tradition (qere) differ slightly here, between "his might" and "his mighty deeds"; the sense is the same, and Balanced says "his power". Thunder is the loudest sound people know, and it stands for the full display of God's power, which no one can take in. The book returns to this in God's speech from the storm (chapters 38-41).

decisions.choice: Who could ever understand his mighty power, which is like thunder?
alternatives: the thunder of his mighty deeds, who will understand?
decisions.reason: Readable puts the question first and explains the picture of thunder as a comparison.
